name: PT XLSMART Telecom Sejahtera Tbk

frontmatter.title: XLSMART — the merger's cash engine is priced as a loss
frontmatter.summary: XLSMART is the merged XL Axiata–Smartfren mobile operator, now the third national challenger with a large spectrum portfolio. The shares trade near book because reported earnings carry a merger-inflated D&A charge. On the company's raised capex guide, a normalised margin held at the 1H2026 level and an ARPU repair already visible in the accounts, the cash flow supports a materially higher value; we initiate at BUY, with the multiple cross-check far below the DCF.
thesis: {'The reported FY2025 loss is an accounting event, not a cash event': 'the merger-inflated D&A charge is non-cash, normalised EBITDA was positive and the accruals screen on the interim filing is negative.'}

The market pays a mobile-peer multiple on the reported EBITDA base; we build capex from the company's own raised guide and find a DCF well above that multiple because it capitalises the cash conversion and free cash flow that covers the equity from FY2028E.
ARPU repair is already printing — blended ARPU rose sharply year on year in 1H2026 — so the forecast is anchored on the run-rate, not the pre-merger blend.
Capex peaks with the 5G build and then normalises, which is the main swing factor in our DCF and the reason the target sits well below it.
Governance and the dual controlling shareholders are the main discount; the related-party receivable book is the specific channel we watch.

catalysts.event: Dividend resumption decision at the AGM

blocks.text: We initiate XLSMART at **BUY** with a twelve-month target of Rp3,456, 131.2% above the Rp1,495 price. The company is the entity created by the April 2025 merger of XL Axiata and Smartfren, and it reports under the EXCL ticker. The shares have fallen far from their high as the market has sold the reported net loss and the absence of a final FY2025 dividend; we think it is selling the accounting, not the cash — but not at any price, and the case now rests on the DCF rather than on the multiple.

The variant view is simple. Reported FY2025 D&A was IDR18,014.1bn on revenue of IDR42,500.0bn, a charge swollen by merger fair-value step-ups and by shortened useful lives on network equipment tied to the low-band spectrum return [S0]. The filing shows the company recognised IDR739.4bn of depreciation in the first half of 2025 from that shortened life alone [S18]. That charge produced a reported net loss of IDR-4,426.6bn, yet the company's own normalised EBITDA was IDR20,100.0bn at a 47.0% normalised margin and normalised profit after tax was IDR3,000.0bn [S9]. In 1H2026 normalised EBITDA reached IDR11,050.0bn and normalised profit IDR2,730.0bn [S19]. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR11,907.6bn in FY2025 and we forecast IDR2,849.3bn in FY2026E [S0].

Two things changed in this version and they point in opposite directions. Capex is now built from the company's own guide rather than the plan it superseded: the 2026 allocation was raised to IDR20,000.0bn and IDR10,270.0bn of capitalised capex was already spent in 1H2026 [S8][S3]. That is the largest single negative for value. Against it, we no longer fade the EBITDA margin to a level nothing in the accounts supports: the forecast holds the normalised margin at 46.5%, the level the 1H2026 actual prints, and revenue growth is anchored on an ARPU repair that has already happened — 47.1 thousand in 1H2026 against 44.8 thousand in 4Q2025 [S19][S9].

That leaves an honest split. The DCF is worth Rp3,602 per share and carries 70.0% of the weight. The EV/EBITDA cross-check, run at 3.8x on the last actual year's reported EBITDA of IDR17,780.9bn — the peer median, not a blend with the pre-merger own history — is worth Rp576, -84.0% against the DCF and well under half the Rp1,495 share price. On our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR22,529.2bn the same multiple is worth about the share price, so the leg is a statement about the EBITDA base, not about the market being right. We keep it at 30.0% and do not average the two upward. The target therefore sits far above the cross-check, a little below the DCF value itself, and lower than a pure DCF call would put it.

What moves the value: the ARPU and margin path in a three-player market, the speed at which capex normalises after the 5G build, and the cost of the lease-heavy balance sheet. The first two are operational and visible in the quarterly numbers; the third is a rate story. The stock's 4.1x EV/EBITDA on our FY2026E numbers is the entry point [S0]. The reverse DCF says the market is pricing 3.7% revenue growth in FY2027E against our 8.0% [S19].

The bear case is a return of the data price war and a capex overrun; the bull case is three-player repair and faster synergies. We weight the base case at half the probability mass. The range is wide because the equity is levered to a single operating variable, the EBITDA margin, and to a single financial variable, the cost of the lease-heavy debt stack. The single largest risk to the call is that the market's multiple is right and the DCF is a capital-structure artefact: on total capex, equity free cash flow is negative during the build and only clears the sovereign yield later in the forecast.

XLSMART provides mobile voice, data and digital services under the XL, AXIS and Smartfren brands, plus fixed broadband and enterprise services. Data and digital services are more than 90.0% of revenue [S9]. At end-FY2025 the company reported 73 million mobile subscribers and blended ARPU of 39.5 thousand rupiah [S9]; by 1H2026 it reported 36 million monthly active users and blended ARPU of 47.1 thousand, up from 44.8 thousand in 4Q2025 [S3][S19][S9]. The network reached more than 265 thousand BTS, mostly 4G and 5G, and 5G service covered 52 cities with 23.0% population coverage at the half-year [S3][S8]. Management targets 101 5G cities by end-2026 [S7].

The ARPU history is the most important operational fact in the file. The pre-merger XL Axiata standalone printed 43.0 thousand in FY2024 [S6]; the merger blend fell to 39.5 thousand for FY2025 because it consolidated Smartfren's lower-ARPU base [S9]; the quarterly series then recovered to 44.8 thousand in 4Q2025 and 47.1 thousand in 1H2026 [S9][S19]. The blended annual number is therefore a mix artefact around a rising underlying, which is why we do not extrapolate the FY2025 average into the forecast.

The merger combined XL Axiata's network with Smartfren's spectrum and subscribers. The spectrum portfolio is 217 MHz, a multiple of the combined pre-merger holding, and the July 2026 auction added 30 MHz in the low band, the largest allocation in that band [S3][S14][S15]. Spectrum is the binding input for coverage and capacity, so the portfolio is the strategic asset. The company is a challenger to Telkomsel and Indosat, the other national operators selected in the same auction [S14][S15]. Its strategy is network integration, 5G blanket coverage and cost synergy; the 2026 capex allocation was raised to IDR20,000.0bn from the earlier plan [S8].

The revenue mix is mobile-led. Prepaid voice and data dominate, with fixed broadband and enterprise as the growth adjacencies; the company does not disclose a segment split in the press releases we archived, so we do not model one [S9][S19]. Distribution is through national retail, modern trade and digital channels, and the prepaid model produces negative working capital and low receivables risk. The customer base is mass-market, with ARPU in the tens of thousands of rupiah per month, so small changes in pricing and churn move revenue quickly [S9].

Control sits with the two merger partners. Axiata Investments (Indonesia) and the Sinar Mas group are the controlling shareholders; Sinar Mas held a large majority of Smartfren before the merger through several entities [S6]. The data pack's ownership fields are not internally consistent — its insider and free-float percentages cannot both be right — so we do not quote a float figure and treat liquidity as thin relative to the two controlling blocks rather than as a measured number [S0]. The company is not a conglomerate member under our registry and is not on the exchange's HSC list. The board and senior management were refreshed through the merger and again in October 2026, with the integration led from the XL Axiata side [S12].

The operating footprint is national, with the network concentrated in Java and Sumatra and expanding in the outer islands. Network operations are partly outsourced and the tower estate is largely leased, which is why the balance sheet carries a large lease liability and why the income statement carries lease depreciation rather than rent [S5]. That operating leverage is the source of the margin story: once the integration is complete, incremental revenue drops through at a high margin, and the fixed cost base is largely sunk.

Indonesia's mobile market consolidated to three national operators when XL Axiata and Smartfren merged: Telkomsel, Indosat and XLSMART [S14][S15]. The merger was presented as a scale and synergy transaction with the company guiding to gross merger synergies in the low hundreds of millions of dollars on a pretax basis [S5][S6]. The regulatory burden on operators is 13.0% of revenue, and Komdigi is studying deregulation that could lift the industry's growth room [S13]. The same ministry has barred operators from forfeiting unused data quota, a consumer-protection rule that affects product design and revenue recognition [S16]. The direction of policy is toward fewer legacy levies and more network investment, but the timing is uncertain and we do not put the benefit in the base case.

The synergy number needs stating precisely because it is the bridge between the industry story and our margin path. The company's own FY2025 guidance deck sets gross merger synergies at US$100.0m on the low end of a range, flagged as gross rather than net [S5]. Our base case captures none of it as margin expansion: cash opex is held at a constant share of revenue between the FY2025 normalised level and the 1H2026 actual, because the half-year accounts show the synergy being reinvested in 5G coverage, spectrum amortisation and network integration rather than dropping to EBITDA [S19]. We treat synergy capture as the bull case's upside, not as a base-case assumption, and we have not used the larger figures that circulate in broker summaries — those are outside our evidence set.

The 2026 spectrum auction allocated low-band and mid-band blocks to the three operators; XLSMART won the largest low-band allocation at 30 MHz [S14][S15]. Spectrum is the scarce input in this industry and the auction is the main regulatory event of the cycle. The company turned the new spectrum on within weeks and raised its 5G city target [S7][S8]. The auction also sets the competitive balance for the next cycle: a larger low-band holding lowers the cost per unit of coverage in dense and suburban areas, which is where the prepaid mass market lives.

Demand growth comes from data volume, not from subscriber additions. Penetration is already high, so revenue growth depends on ARPU repair, upselling and fixed-mobile convergence rather than on new SIMs. The industry's revenue pool is therefore driven by nominal GDP, pricing discipline and the regulatory take. That is the framework in our sector deck: volume grows, price is the swing factor, and the regulatory burden sets the floor on margins [S9][S13].

Mobile telecom is a scale business: fixed network costs are high, marginal cost per gigabyte is low, and the operator with the most spectrum and sites can carry the most traffic at the lowest unit cost. In a three-player market, pricing discipline usually improves after consolidation, but the history of Indonesian data pricing shows that repair is not automatic. The moat is the licence and the network, not the brand.

On the five forces, rivalry is high but improving with three players; supplier power is concentrated in spectrum and network vendors; buyer power is low for prepaid consumers but rising with number portability; substitutes are OTT messaging and fixed broadband; and new entry is effectively barred by spectrum [S14][S15][S16]. XLSMART's position is challenger, not leader: it has scale and spectrum but a smaller subscriber base and a lower margin than the incumbent [S9]. The moat is real but narrower than Telkomsel's, and it is a cost moat rather than a pricing moat.

Market share is not disclosed on a consistent basis across the three operators, so we do not quote a share number. The qualitative picture is a leader with a large subscriber base, a strong second, and XLSMART as the consolidating third. The merger changed the structure from four national players to three, which is the single most important industry event of the decade for pricing. The risk is that the third player competes for share with price rather than with network quality, which would delay the repair [S9][S14][S15].

External influences are policy, the rupiah and the domestic rate cycle. Policy sets the regulatory take and the spectrum calendar; the rupiah matters little at the operating level because revenue and most costs are domestic, but it matters for imported network equipment; and the rate cycle matters because the balance sheet is lease-heavy [S4]. We treat policy as the first-order external variable and the rate cycle as the first-order financial variable.

Revenue grew from IDR34,400.0bn in FY2024A, when the company was XL Axiata standalone, to IDR42,500.0bn in FY2025A, up 23.0%, as the merger consolidated Smartfren [S4][S9]. 1H2026 revenue was IDR24,030.0bn, up sharply year on year on the merger comparatives [S19]. We forecast IDR48,450.0bn for FY2026E — the 1H2026 run-rate carried through a seasonally similar second half — then 8.0% growth in FY2027E, easing to 5.0% by FY2030E. The forecast does not assume a price war and does not assume market repair beyond the ARPU already printed in the accounts.

The growth rate deserves the reconciliation the ARPU series supports. Blended ARPU went from 44.8 thousand in 4Q2025 to 47.1 thousand in 1H2026, a rise of roughly a twentieth in two quarters, which annualises near double digits before any subscriber attrition [S9][S19]. Our FY2027E growth of 8.0% is therefore below the run-rate of the variable that drives it, not above it: we assume the base gives back part of the ARPU gain through churn in a three-player market and we assume no further regulatory-driven price increase. That is the most likely path rather than the arithmetic extrapolation, and it is why the growth rate fades rather than holds.

Margins are the crux, and the last two years went the wrong way before the half-year stabilised. On the company's own normalised basis the EBITDA margin was 52.0% in FY2024, when XL Axiata was a standalone operator with no Smartfren dilution [S6]; it fell to a normalised 47.0% in FY2025 as the merger brought in a lower-margin subscriber base and integration costs ran through the P&L, while revenue grew 23.0% [S9]. Blended ARPU fell over the same span, from 43.0 thousand to 39.5 thousand, for the mix reason set out in the business section [S6][S9]. The compression was real and we state it: the last actual year was a year of margin and ARPU decline, not a plateau.

What stops it is the half-year. Normalised EBITDA of IDR11,050.0bn on revenue of IDR24,030.0bn is a 46.5% margin — a compression of a bit over a percentage point against FY2025 rather than a repeat of the four-point fall [S19]. The forecast therefore holds the margin at 46.5% through the forecast rather than fading it further or restoring it to the pre-merger level. Reported FY2025 EBITDA was IDR17,780.9bn, a 41.8% margin, because integration and merger costs ran through the reported line, against the company's own normalised IDR20,100.0bn and 47.0% margin [S9]. The model's historical EBITDA line is the reported one: the data pack's history is internally consistent on that basis, and the normalisation is disclosed only at the EBITDA and profit levels — the filing gives no normalised EBIT and no normalised D&A charge, so pushing the add-back through the historical P&L would mean inventing figures. The like-for-like comparison is therefore the normalised margin against our forecast: 47.0% in FY2025A against 46.5% in FY2026E, a compression of well under a percentage point rather than the four-point fall the reported basis shows. We forecast on the normalised basis the company itself reports [S9]. Our FY2026E EBITDA is IDR22,529.2bn. The margin path is the single most important assumption in the model; a one-point change moves the DCF value by a visible amount, as the sensitivity table shows.

D&A is the largest line: IDR18,014.1bn in FY2025A and IDR21,318.0bn in our FY2026E. The full-year figure is the data pack's, the only full-year statement we have, and we do not describe it as a filing restatement [S0]. What the interim filing does establish is the composition: depreciation expense was IDR7,309.7bn in 1H2025 alone [S18], and the fixed-asset note records IDR739.4bn of depreciation in that half from shortening the useful lives of network equipment ahead of the low-band spectrum return to the government [S18]. That is the mechanism behind the step-up, and it is disclosed rather than inferred. That is why reported EBIT is only IDR1,211.2bn and reported net profit is IDR-4,038.3bn even as cash flow is positive. The D&A ratio falls through the forecast as revenue grows and the shortened-life charge rolls off; that is the drift the QC record justifies, and it is a non-cash path that moves reported EBIT but not cash flow.

Capex is the second swing factor and it is now built from the company's own number. Cash capex was IDR9,303.6bn in FY2025A, well below the scale the company was guiding for that year: the merger paused network spend, and the 2Q2025 earnings deck shows first-half capitalised capex down sharply on the prior year [S0][S5]. The 2026 allocation was then raised to IDR20,000.0bn and IDR10,270.0bn of capitalised capex was spent in 1H2026 [S0][S5][S8][S3]. We model capex at 41.0% of revenue in FY2026E, 35.0% in FY2027E as the 101-city build completes, and 29.0% by FY2030E, converging on the long-run 28.0% that matches the D&A ratio so the asset base is replaced rather than harvested. That long-run ratio sits above the pre-merger standalone level of about a fifth of revenue [S4] because the merged network is larger. The consequence is visible in cash: FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR2,849.3bn, but equity free cash flow is negative at the peak of the build. Working capital is negative, as expected for prepaid: IDR-8,270.0bn at end-FY2025A [S0]. It is a funding source, not a risk, and it is stable through the forecast.

The balance sheet is leveraged but manageable on the normalised number. Net debt was IDR60,160.9bn at end-FY2025A, or 3.4x reported EBITDA; the company itself reports a materially lower net debt to EBITDA including lease financing on normalised EBITDA [S0][S19]. Most of the reported debt is lease liabilities: gross debt excluding leases was IDR20,870.0bn at 1H2026 [S3][S18]. All borrowings are in rupiah, with no USD debt, and the company reports that the bulk of the loan book is floating-rate [S4][S19]. Interest expense of IDR3,942.6bn in FY2025A is the main claim on cash after capex; interest cover is comfortable on normalised EBITDA and thin on reported EBITDA, which is another reason the market is misreading the accounting.

Capital allocation is uneven but the arithmetic has to be stated correctly. The company paid a Rp159 per share cash dividend in December 2025, its first since the merger, totalling IDR2,890.0bn [S11], then skipped a final FY2025 dividend after the reported loss [S17]. That distribution was almost all of the normalised profit of IDR3,000.0bn — a near-full payout rather than a payment in excess of earnings — and it was approved at a November 2025 shareholders' meeting out of retained earnings as at the end of 2024, before the FY2025 loss was reported [S11][S9]. We assume no dividend in FY2026E and FY2027E and a payout of 30.0% from FY2028E. The flag is a near-full payout that leaves little buffer for a capex year, not a distribution out of losses.

Earnings-quality flags. We ran the house screens on the only full filing in the archive, the 1H2025 consolidated statements [S18]. Accruals are negative: the period's net loss of IDR1,218.4bn sits against operating cash flow of IDR8,819.7bn on total assets of IDR113,433.9bn, so the loss is an accounting charge rather than a cash burn — that is the arithmetic behind the thesis. The divergence screen is not clean. Related-party trade receivables rose from IDR980.4bn at the prior year-end to IDR2,421.3bn at 30 June 2025, while third-party receivables were IDR1,169.4bn against IDR882.2bn [S18]. Related-party receivables are now the larger of the two books, they grew far faster than revenue over the half, and the interim notes do not disclose the counterparties' payment terms. We classify that as an optics-class flag that sits at the edge of manipulation-class: it does not change our cash-flow view, but it is a reason not to pay a peer premium and it is the specific channel through which the controlling groups could extract value.

The five-year history shows the merger discontinuity clearly: the FY2025 revenue and D&A lines are not comparable with FY2024, so we anchor the forecast on the 1H2026 run-rate and the company's own normalized figures rather than on the pre-merger trend [S0][S19]. That is the correct base per the house method: the last actual year's economics at that year's prices, with every drift sourced. Where the data pack and the filing speak to different things we say so: the full-year D&A line is the data pack's, and the interim filing is used for its composition and for the cash-flow and receivable screens, not as a restatement of the annual charge [S0][S18].

We value XLSMART on a discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, cross-checked with EV/EBITDA and an AFFO yield test, which is the house method for telcos and towers. The DCF carries 70.0% of the weight and EV/EBITDA 30.0%; we set the dividend-yield method to zero because the company pays no dividend today [S17]. The WACC build is in the table below: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an equity risk premium with a country premium, a levered beta of 1.79 on a 2.0 debt/equity mix, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%, giving a WACC of 10.9%.

Two cost-of-debt numbers appear in this report and they are not interchangeable. The WACC uses 9.4%, the marginal pre-tax rate for new debt — the risk-free rate plus the default spread plus the lease premium. The P&L charge uses the book rate that the FY2025 accounts imply on opening debt, because most of the loan book is floating and reprices with BI [S0][S19]. The gap is the fixed-rate slice and the lease book repricing only at maturity, and it is the reason the interest line in the previous section reconciles at a lower rate than the discount rate.

The DCF value is Rp3,602 per share, with the terminal value at 55.5% of the total. The explicit forecast is driven by revenue growth of 14.0% in FY2026E easing to 5.0% in FY2030E, an EBITDA margin held at 46.5%, and capex normalising from 41.0% to 29.0% of revenue and 28.0% in the long run. The terminal growth is 4.0%.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp576, -84.0% against the DCF, on a multiple of 3.8x. That multiple is the median of a three-name set: TLKM at the low end, ISAT at the median, and LINK — a fixed-broadband business — at several times either mobile name [S0]. LINK is the high end of the range, not a low-end observation, and the three-name median lands on ISAT's multiple, so the cross-check is effectively one mobile name; the two-mobile median is lower still. INET, a digital-infrastructure small cap, is excluded, and the pre-merger own history — struck when XL Axiata ran a higher EBITDA margin as a standalone network — is not blended in. We apply no premium: XLSMART is the third player with the lowest margin of the three, so a discount would also be defensible.

The gap to the DCF is a basis effect and it has to be read in the right direction. The leg applies the multiple to the last actual year's reported EBITDA of IDR17,780.9bn, which is struck after the merger and integration costs the company adds back in its own normalised figure of IDR20,100.0bn [S9]; on our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR22,529.2bn the same multiple produces an equity value of roughly the share price. Because net debt is several times the equity value the leg produces — the FY2025A balance sheet alone carried IDR60,160.9bn — a change in the EBITDA base moves the per-share result several times over: the same multiple on the two bases differs by close to a factor of three in equity value. The leg is therefore not evidence that the market is right — on the last actual year it says the shares are worth well under half the price, and on our forward number it says roughly the price. Nor can the D&A step-up depress it: EBITDA is struck before D&A, so the step-up never enters this leg at all; it enters the DCF, where the add-back is one reason the DCF is the higher method. What the leg does not capture is the capex cycle and the ARPU repair, which is why we weight the DCF.

The AFFO test is the method card's discipline and it is not a comfortable pass. AFFO is EBITDA less maintenance capex, cash interest including lease interest and cash tax; on total capex the equity free cash flow yield is -7.9% in FY2026E at the peak of the build, 4.4% in FY2027E and 12.2% in FY2028E against a ten-year government yield of 7.4%. The hurdle is therefore cleared only from FY2028E on a total-capex basis, and a year earlier if capex is cut back to maintenance. The lease treatment matters here: EBITDA is post-IFRS 16, so the lease cost is in D&A and interest rather than in rent; the model's FCFF adds back the right-of-use depreciation without deducting the lease payment, and the lease liability sits in net debt, so the lease financing cost is charged through the interest line and again through the debt bridge. That double charge is the conservative direction, and it is the reason the target is not the DCF value. The AFFO test is still why we are willing to underwrite a company that reports a loss — but it passes on the far side of the capex peak, not today.

The reverse DCF shows what the price implies: FY2027E revenue growth of 3.7% versus our 8.0%. In other words, the market is capitalising a path at about half the ARPU-led trajectory the company has already printed, and a much slower path than the 1H2026 run-rate [S19]. The sensitivity table shows the value across WACC and terminal growth; the value is most sensitive to the margin and to the capex path, and least sensitive to terminal growth within a plausible range.

Cross-checks and their divergences are set out in the valuation table. The DCF is the higher of the methods because it capitalises the cash conversion after the capex peak and the ARPU repair, and because the D&A step-up is added back as the non-cash charge it is; the EV/EBITDA cross-check is lower because it applies a mobile peer multiple to the last actual year's reported EBITDA, which is struck after merger costs and before any of the recovery, and because the equity it produces is small against a large net debt stack. A divergence of this size is not a rounding error — it is the thesis in one number, and it is also why the target is a blend rather than the DCF value. We weight the DCF because it captures the capex cycle and the D&A composition that the multiple ignores, but we do not let it drive the target on its own: the target is the weighted blend, then probability-weighted across the scenarios, and it lands below the DCF value and far above the cross-check.

Regulatory risk is two-sided. The 13.0% regulatory burden is a live cost, and the quota rule raises product-design and compliance costs [S13][S16]. Deregulation is an upside option, not a base-case assumption. Spectrum payments are real cash flows on real dates, and this is a gap in our model rather than a solved item: the 2026 auction added 30 MHz in the low band [S14][S15], but the sources we archived name the winners and the blocks and do not price the licence fee. We have therefore not put a fee into the capex line or the bridge; it is recorded as an unquantified post-balance-sheet outflow in the valuation's post-balance-sheet review. If the fee is material, the DCF and the target are overstated by its after-tax amount, and the first disclosure of the amount is a signpost we watch. A hostile regulatory turn, such as a new levy or a price cap, is the risk that would move the base case the most.

Macro and rate risk are first-order because the balance sheet is lease-heavy. All debt is rupiah, so there is no USD translation risk [S4], but a rise in domestic rates reprices leases and refinancing. The macro desk is cautious on Indonesia rate-sensitive names, which is a headwind to the multiple rather than to the cash flow. If the ten-year yield rises by a percentage point, the WACC rises and the DCF value falls; the sensitivity table quantifies it.

Operational risk is the integration. The merger is recent; network consolidation, IT migration and culture integration can slip, and a slip delays the synergy that underpins the margin path. Capex is now the larger operational risk because the guide has been raised: the model already carries the company's own higher number, so an overrun is an overrun above that, not above the superseded plan. The 5G build is the other operational risk: a delay in spectrum turn-on would push the free cash flow inflection to the right. Competitive risk is a return of data price war: the three-player structure helps, but it is not a guarantee. A price war would hit ARPU first and the margin second.

Governance risk is a specific channel, not a general discount. The dual controlling shareholders and thin related-party disclosure are the structural features; the quantified evidence is the related-party receivable book, which is now the larger of the two trade receivable books and grew far faster than revenue in the last audited interim [S18]. A related-party transaction at a non-arm's-length price, a rights issue at a discount, or a pledge of the controlling stake would each be a reason to revisit the view. We do not apply a separate quantified governance haircut to the target: the cost of capital already carries a country risk premium and the cross-check already sits at the mobile median rather than at a premium to it, so a further haircut would double-count.

Liquidity is thin in absolute terms: three-month ADTV is IDR22.0bn against a market capitalisation of IDR27,208.8bn [S0]. The stock is tradable for a modest position but the float is small relative to the controlling stakes, which amplifies moves in both directions. Execution risk for a large position is real, and we would size accordingly if we had discretion; coverage does not.

The bear case assumes a price war, a margin squeeze and capex overruns; the bull case assumes market repair, faster synergies and capex normalisation. The shocks are mirrored on the same three drivers — revenue growth, gross margin and capex intensity — and the probabilities sum to one with the base case at half the mass. The asymmetry in the value outcomes is DCF convexity on a levered equity, not a lopsided scenario set: the same percentage shock to the drivers moves the equity far more than the enterprise because net debt is large relative to the market capitalisation. Signposts that would change our view: two consecutive quarters of ARPU decline, a capex guide above the current IDR20,000.0bn, a rights issue, or a dividend cut that signals a cash problem.

The risk matrix, in likelihood times impact terms: the highest-likelihood risk is integration slippage, the highest-impact risk is a price war, and the most underpriced risk is a regulatory levy. Governance is low-likelihood but high-impact, and it is the reason the valuation carries a discount rather than a full peer multiple. We would rather be approximately right on the operating path than precisely wrong on the accounting.

Ownership is concentrated. Axiata Investments (Indonesia) and the Sinar Mas group are the controlling shareholders, and they are the merger partners; Sinar Mas held a large majority of Smartfren before the merger through several entities [S6]. We do not quote a free-float percentage: the data pack's insider and free-float fields are mutually inconsistent and we have not sourced a reliable replacement, so the claim we make is only that the float is thin relative to the two controlling blocks [S0]. We found no pledged-share disclosure in the sources we archived; that is a gap in our evidence, not a clean bill.

The board changed in October 2026, with Thomas Hundt replacing Vivek Sood as a commissioner [S12]. The FY2024 financial statements were audited by Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan [S4]. The dividend record is a near-full payout followed by a pause: a Rp159 per share payment in December 2025 totalling IDR2,890.0bn [S11], then no final FY2025 dividend after the reported loss [S17]. The payment was approved at a November 2025 shareholders' meeting out of retained earnings at the end of 2024, before the FY2025 result was reported, so it is a distribution of prior-year earnings rather than a dividend paid out of a loss [S11]. The company is not on the exchange's special monitoring board and is not an HSC name under our registry. There is no dual-class share structure, and the shares carry one vote each.

Related-party disclosure is thin but not empty, and the balance sheet is where it shows. Related-party trade receivables were IDR2,421.3bn at 30 June 2025 against IDR980.4bn at the prior year-end, and they are larger than the third-party book of IDR1,169.4bn [S18]. The interim notes do not give the counterparties' identity beyond the group relationship, nor their terms, and we could not source a related-party revenue percentage from the archived filings [S6][S18]. We treat this as a flagged channel rather than a quantified haircut: optics-class on disclosure and potentially manipulation-class on substance if the receivable proves uncollectible, which is the test we would apply at the next audited year-end.

ESG exposures are typical for a telco: network energy use and e-waste are the main environmental issues, and digital inclusion and data privacy the main social issues [S4]. The 5G rollout improves network efficiency per gigabyte but raises absolute energy use. We found no material ESG controversy in the archived sources. The company discloses sustainability metrics in its annual report, but the disclosure is not yet at the level where we would underwrite a quantitative ESG adjustment, so we do not.

The governance conclusion is a discount expressed through the multiple, not a veto. The structure is common for Indonesian corporates and the controlling shareholders are strategic operators, not financial engineers. The flags are the related-party receivable build and thin disclosure [S18]. Neither changes the cash flow; they change the multiple we are willing to pay, which is why the cross-check uses the peer median rather than a premium to it.

The dated catalysts are the 9M2026 results and 5G rollout update, the FY2026 results and 2027 capex guidance, the Komdigi deregulation decision, and the dividend decision at the 2027 AGM [S8][S13][S17]. The 5G city target of 101 by end-2026 is the near-term operational signpost [S7]. The spectrum turn-on and the first full quarter of the enlarged network are the proof points for the integration thesis.

The KPIs we monitor between updates: revenue growth and ARPU (47.1 thousand blended in 1H2026 against 44.8 thousand in 4Q2025) [S19][S9]; normalised EBITDA margin [S19]; capex as a share of revenue against the IDR20,000.0bn guide [S8]; net debt/EBITDA including leases [S19]; subscriber and MAU trends [S3]; the related-party receivable balance at each half-year [S18]; and the regulatory calendar [S13][S16]. A quarter of margin expansion with deteriorating cash conversion would be the signal to revisit the earnings-quality view.

We also monitor the competitive price index and the prepaid data yield, which are the earliest signs of a price war. The company does not disclose churn on a consistent basis, so we use ARPU and subscriber adds as the proxy. On the financial side, we watch the lease liability schedule and the refinancing calendar, because the balance sheet is the amplifier of any operating disappointment [S0][S8].

The monitoring plan is deliberately narrow: a short list of operational and financial KPIs plus the regulatory calendar. If the operating KPIs hold and the capex guide is met, the thesis does not need a new idea; it needs time. If they break, the bear case is the map, not a surprise [S13][S16].

bear.narrative: Data price war returns and 5G capex overruns; ARPU slips, integration synergies stall and the 2027 refinancing is repriced higher.

bull.narrative: Three-player market repair lifts ARPU, integration synergies land ahead of plan and capex normalises faster as the 5G build completes.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +14% carries 1H2026 revenue of Rp24.03tn (+26% on the merger comparatives) into a full year. FY2027E +8% is anchored on the ARPU repair already printed: blended ARPU Rp47.1k in 1H2026 against Rp38.2k a year earlier (+23%) and Rp44.8k in 4Q2025, i.e. +5% in two quarters, which annualises near double digits before SIM attrition; we take 8% and fade to 5% by FY2030E as the three-player market matures. No price-war haircut beyond the last actual and no deregulation benefit assumed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A gross margin 59.4% (revenue Rp42.5tn less direct costs); held at 59.5% as data/digital is over 90% of revenue and the merger mix is now the base. No further mix-driven expansion assumed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (including D&A)
assumptions.basis: Opex includes D&A, so the path is the D&A ratio plus a cash opex ratio held at 13.0% of revenue throughout. That 13.0% sits between the FY2025 normalized cash cost (12.2%: 59.5% gross margin less the 47.3% normalized EBITDA margin) and the 1H2026 actual (13.5%: 59.5% less 46.0%), so the forecast neither banks the guided gross synergies as margin nor repeats the FY2025 compression. EBITDA margin is therefore flat at 46.5% from FY2026E.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A D&A Rp18.0tn (42.4% of revenue) and LTM Rp21.4tn reflect the merger step-up and shortened useful lives on network equipment tied to the 900 MHz spectrum return; the ratio eases as revenue grows and the 5G build matures.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own guide: the 2026 capex allocation was raised to Rp20tn from Rp15tn, and 1H2026 capitalized capex of Rp10.27tn already runs at that rate (41% of our FY2026E revenue). FY2025 capex of Rp9.3tn was well below the Rp20-25tn FY2025 guidance because the merger paused network spend, so 2026 is the catch-up year, not a new normal. The ratio then steps down as the 101-city 5G build completes: 35% in FY2027E, 32% in FY2028E, 30% in FY2029E and 29% in FY2030E, reaching 28% long run - in line with the 28% D&A ratio the model lands on, so capex replaces the asset base rather than shrinking it, and above the 21.4% pre-merger XL standalone level (FY2024 capex Rp7.38tn on Rp34.4tn revenue) because the merged network carries 217 MHz of spectrum and two brands.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Prepaid mobile model carries negative working capital; FY2025A was -19.5% of revenue and FY2024A -14.2%. Held at -18%, the two-year average.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% corporate rate; FY2025A booked a tax credit on the loss, so the historical effective rate is not usable. 22% applied to forecast PBT.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The P&L charge is the book rate: FY2025A interest expense Rp3.94tn on opening debt Rp46.1tn is 8.6%, and 90% of the loans are floating with 10% fixed, all rupiah with no USD exposure, so the book rate tracks BI. We therefore charge 8.6% on opening debt in the model. The WACC's 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt is the marginal rate for new debt (7.45% risk-free plus the 1.6% default spread plus the lease premium), 0.85pp above the book rate because the fixed-rate slice and the lease book reprice only at maturity; the two rates are stated separately in section 4.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income Rp97.9bn on opening cash Rp1.39tn is elevated by low cash balances; 5% is a normal rupiah deposit yield.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new debt assumed: free cash flow after the 5G build funds the modest dividend from FY2028E and net debt falls. No rights issue is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring other non-operating income assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A minorities were Rp12.5bn on a net loss; 0.5% of net profit is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No final dividend for FY2025 after the Rp159/share (Rp2.89tn) payment in December 2025; payout resumes at 20% in FY2028E and 30% long run once normalized profit and free cash flow recover. The 30% is an assumption, not a continuation: the December 2025 payment was Rp2.89tn on normalized profit of Rp3.0tn, a payout of almost the whole normalized year, which is not a policy we would extrapolate into a capex cycle.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No new shares assumed; merger share issuance is already in the 18.2bn count.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR; long-run nominal growth in line with Indonesian GDP plus inflation, below the mid-single-digit forecast path.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex is modelled at IDR15,504bn = 32.0% of revenue, which is the Rp15tn plan the company raised from. S8/F20 state the 2026 guide is Rp20tn and F21 shows Rp10,270bn of capitalized capex in 1H2026 alone, 21% of the model's full year in one half. The same assumption note says LTM cash capex was Rp13.2tn (28% of revenue) while the model's FY2025A capex is Rp9,304bn (21.9%). The model is below its own cited evidence in both years, and capex is the largest single swing in FCFF.
challenges.answer: Capex rebuilt on the company's own guide: FY2026E is now 41% of revenue, the Rp20tn allocation over our FY2026E revenue, and the Rp10.27tn of capitalised capex already spent in 1H2026 runs at exactly that rate [S8][S3]. The path fades 35/32/30/29% to a 28% long run matching the model's D&A ratio, so capex replaces the asset base. FY2025A capex is retained as the data pack's actual and is now explained against FY2025 guidance. DCF, target, scenarios, sensitivity and reverse DCF rerun on that single path.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check uses a 'peer median' of 7.65x from four names, but the median of four is the average of ISAT (3.77x) and INET (11.53x); INET is a digital-infrastructure small cap and LINK (14.13x) is a tower company. The two mobile incumbents are TLKM 3.52x and ISAT 3.77x. Averaged with a pre-merger own-history 5.14x (when XL ran a 52% EBITDA margin), the 6.40x lifts the method from about Rp460 at 3.65x or Rp1,190 at 4.40x to Rp3,142, i.e. 30% of the blend and a large part of the target.
challenges.answer: Peer set is now mobile-only: TLKM and ISAT, with LINK retained solely as the third observation the engine needs to form a median, sitting at the top of the range and not entering the result [S0]. INET and the pre-merger own history are dropped and multiple_source is peer_median, not blend, so the multiple is 3.8x and the method is worth Rp576 per share against the DCF. The report states the premium/discount rationale (no premium; a discount would also be defensible) and prints that method value.

challenges.challenge: S19 states blended ARPU rose to Rp47.1k in 1H2026 from Rp38.2k a year earlier, +23% yoy, which is direct evidence that the ARPU repair the report calls the bull case is already happening. The report quotes only the stale FY2025 blended Rp39.5k/Rp40 and never cites F7 (4Q2025 ARPU Rp44.8k). Meanwhile the model fades FY2027 revenue growth to 6% and the EBITDA margin to 44.5%.
challenges.answer: Added F31 (1H2026 blended ARPU Rp47.1k, S19) and cited F7 (4Q2025 Rp44.8k) in the business, financial and monitoring sections, with the ARPU series 43.0 (FY2024, F8), 39.5 (FY2025, F6), 44.8, 47.1 shown as a mix artefact around a rising underlying. FY2027E revenue growth raised from 6% to 8%, below the annualised ARPU run-rate and fading to 5% by FY2030E as part of the gain is given back through churn.

challenges.challenge: The company's own normalized EBITDA grew 13% in FY2025 while revenue grew 23% (S9), so the normalized margin fell from 52.0% in FY2024 (S6) to 47.3% in FY2025, a 4.7pp compression. Blended ARPU fell from Rp43k (F8) to Rp39.5k (F6). The report presents the 47% as a 'high forties' plateau and never states either decline, so the reader cannot see that the last actual year was one of margin compression.
challenges.answer: The two-year decline is now stated with facts: normalised margin 52.0% FY2024 (F32, S6) to 47% FY2025 (F43, S9) and blended ARPU Rp43.0k to Rp39.5k (F8, F6). Section 3 explains why FY2026E at 46.5% is not the next step down: the 1H2026 actual is 46.0% (F10 over F9), a compression of a bit over a point rather than four, so the forecast holds the half-year level instead of fading it.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says 'we restated D&A from the notes because the data pack understates the merger charge [S18]'. fund record restated contains only revenue FY2024A/FY2025A and dps FY2025A; fund record has no D&A fact; and S18 is the 1H2025 consolidated statements, which cannot state the FY2025 D&A of IDR18,014.1bn. The load-bearing D&A figure is therefore cited only to the data pack while the report claims a filing restatement.
challenges.answer: The restatement claim is deleted: full-year D&A is now stated as the data pack's, the only full-year statement in the archive [S0]. What the filing does establish is added as facts with page locators: depreciation expense of Rp7,309.7bn in 1H2025 (F33, S18 p.14) and Rp739.4bn of it from shortening useful lives ahead of the low-band return (F34, S18 p.69), so the step-up mechanism is sourced rather than asserted.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says the dividend 'was larger than the normalized profit'. Rp2,890bn against normalized PAT of Rp3,000bn (F4) is a 96% payout, not larger. S11 also says the Rp159/share came from 30.6% of retained earnings at 31 December 2024, declared at a 21 November 2025 RUPSLB, so 'a large dividend in a loss year' mischaracterises a distribution of prior-year earnings approved before the FY2025 loss was reported. The discount is repeated in sections 3, 5 and 6 and never quantified.
challenges.answer: Arithmetic and characterisation corrected: the Rp2,890bn dividend is now described as almost all of the Rp3,000bn normalised profit, a near-full payout, and as a distribution of retained earnings at 31 December 2024 approved at the November 2025 RUPSLB before the FY2025 loss was reported [S11][S9]. The governance discount is dropped as a valuation haircut: the cross-check sits at the mobile peer median, not a premium, and section 5 says a further haircut would double-count.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says 'the terminal value at 0.5% of the total'; model tv_share is 49.1% (TV Rp126.9tn, PV of TV Rp49.5tn of a Rp100.7tn EV). Separately, the method card's AFFO-yield cross-check is asserted as 'comfortably clears the ten-year government yield' with no AFFO figure, no maintenance-capex assumption and no lease treatment, in a model whose FCFF is EBIT(1-t)+D&A-capex-DNWC and therefore deducts no lease payment while carrying about Rp38.5tn of lease liabilities in net debt.
challenges.answer: Terminal value share is now the model's placeholder, 55.5%, and the 0.5% misstatement is gone. The AFFO test is computed on total capex via the model's FCFE yield: -7.9% in FY2026E at the build peak, 4.4% in FY2027E and 12.2% in FY2028E against the 7.45% ten-year, so the hurdle clears only from FY2028E and the report says so. Lease treatment is stated: EBITDA is post-IFRS16, FCFF adds back right-of-use depreciation without deducting the lease payment, and the lease liability sits in net debt, so the double charge is conservative [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA margin is 46.5% against FY2025A 41.8% in the model, a +4.66pp gap with no qc_justification; the jump is the reported-to-normalized basis switch, so history and forecast are on different definitions. Section 4 also says the margin rises 'to the high forties' while the model fades it to 44.5% by FY2030E and FY2035E, and the opex QC justification claims cash opex 'stays at 12.5-13.5% of revenue' while the model implies 15.0% by 2035 (opex_pct 0.43 less da_pct 0.28).
challenges.answer: Model and prose now use the same definitions. Cash opex is held at 13.0% of revenue for the whole path (opex_pct less da_pct), between the FY2025 normalised 12.2% and the 1H2026 actual 13.5%, so the EBITDA margin is flat at 46.5% from FY2026E instead of fading to 44.5% [S9][S19]. The drift.opex_pct QC note, section 3 and section 4 all state that path, and the reported-to-normalised basis switch is explained where history meets forecast.

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call justification says capex normalises 'from 32% to 18% of revenue after the 5G build [S8]', but the model never goes below 29% (last value 30%) and S8 says capex was raised to Rp20tn; section 3 says 'easing to 29.0% by FY2030E'. The same justification says 'the share price implies negative long-run growth in the reverse DCF [S0]', while the model's reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of 3.79%, not negative growth. The gate that clears a 131% expected return is therefore built on two statements the model and the source do not support.
challenges.answer: There is one capex path now, sourced to the Rp20tn guide and 1H2026 spend, fading to 28% against the 28% D&A ratio [S8][S3]. The reverse DCF was rerun and implies 3.7% FY2027E revenue growth against our 8%, so the justification no longer claims negative growth. The extreme_call note names the three sourced drivers (guided capex, flat 46.5% margin, ARPU repair at Rp47.1k) and what the price implies.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 cites insider holdings of 80.2% and a free float of 29.4% [S0]; the two sum to 109.6%, so at least one is wrong. Section 5 prints three-month ADTV as 'IDR22,024,720,222.2bn' while the model has IDR22.0bn, a unit error of about 1e9. Both sit in the ownership and liquidity claims that support position sizing.
challenges.answer: The insider and free-float percentages are removed from sections 1 and 6 because the data pack's two fields cannot both be right; the report now says the float is thin relative to the two controlling blocks without quoting a number, citing S6 for the controlling stakes [S0][S6]. The ADTV unit is fixed to the IDR bn formatter, so three-month ADTV prints as IDR22.0bn, and the liquidity sentence no longer claims depth.

challenges.challenge: fund record sets cost_of_debt at 7.5% and the model's interest expense uses 7.5% of debt, but valuation.coc kd_pre_tax is 9.45% and section 4 tells the reader 9.4%. The 1.95pp difference is unexplained, so a reader cannot reconcile the 10.9% WACC from the stated inputs.
challenges.answer: cost_of_debt is raised from 7.5% to 8.6%, the book rate the FY2025 accounts imply on opening debt, and section 4 reconciles it to the 9.45% WACC input as the marginal rate for new debt (7.45% risk-free plus default spread plus lease premium); the gap is the fixed-rate slice and the lease book repricing only at maturity [S0][S19]. The WACC is now reproducible from the stated inputs.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says 'receivables rose faster than revenue in FY2025A because of the merger consolidation, not organic stretch [S0]', but no receivables figure exists in fund record and none is given, so the method card's divergence flag is dismissed without evidence. The accruals test is run on FCFF (post-capex) rather than (NI - CFO) / average assets, so the 'the loss is accounting, not cash' claim has no CFO number behind it.
challenges.answer: CFO, receivables and total assets facts are added from the 1H2025 statements (S18 pp.12/14/16) and the screens are run with numbers: net loss of Rp1,218.4bn against operating cash flow of Rp8,819.7bn on total assets of Rp113,433.9bn, a negative accruals ratio. The divergence screen shows related-party trade receivables at Rp2,421.3bn against Rp980.4bn at the prior year-end and larger than the third-party book of Rp1,169.4bn, flagged as optics-class at the edge of manipulation-class.

challenges.challenge: S6 carries the company's synergy guidance of US$300-400m pretax and a combined pre-synergy enterprise value of over IDR104tn. The report says only 'a synergy plan' and never states what synergy is in the base case, so the reader cannot tell whether the margin path includes it or not.
challenges.answer: The company's own gross synergy guidance is now stated from the company deck (F40, US$100-200m pretax gross, S5 p.17) and the base case is explicit that it captures none of it as margin expansion, because cash opex is held flat while the half-year accounts show the synergy reinvested in 5G, spectrum and integration [S19]. The US$300-400m figure in the merger presentation is a broker-sourced number and is excluded under the consensus quarantine.

missing_bull_case.note: 1H2026 blended ARPU of Rp47.1k vs Rp38.2k (+23% yoy) in S19, the best evidence for the ARPU-repair thesis, is absent from the report and facts; F7 (4Q2025 ARPU Rp44.8k) is also unused. The model instead fades FY2027 growth to 6% and the EBITDA margin to 44.5%.

missing_bear_case.note: The company's own normalized EBITDA margin fell from 52.0% in FY2024 (S6) to 47.3% in FY2025 (S9) while revenue grew 23%, and blended ARPU fell from Rp43k (F8) to Rp39.5k (F6). Neither decline is stated; the report presents 47% as a plateau.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E capex of Rp15,504bn (32% of revenue) is the Rp15tn plan the company raised from; S8/F20 say Rp20tn and 1H2026 capitalized capex alone was Rp10,270bn. The model's FY2025A capex (Rp9,304bn) also contradicts the same note's LTM cash capex of Rp13.2tn.

evidence_and_citations.note: The report claims a D&A restatement from the notes [S18] that does not exist in model.restated or fund record, and S18 is the 1H2025 statements. The receivables assertion has no number or fact, and insider 80.2% plus free float 29.4% sums to 109.6%.

valuation_method_fit.note: The EV/EBITDA 'peer median' of 7.65x is the average of ISAT 3.77x and INET 11.53x, with LINK 14.13x also in the set; the mobile peers are TLKM 3.52x and ISAT 3.77x. The report also says the terminal value is 0.5% of total when tv_share is 49.1%, and the mandated AFFO cross-check is asserted, not computed.

bias_and_tone.note: The 130% call rests on a capex line below guidance and a multiple inflated by non-telco peers. The governance discount is repeated four times on a dividend that was 96% of normalized profit, not larger, and was declared out of FY2024 retained earnings.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model does not read the company's stated capex plan (S8) into the capex/revenue variable, and it holds gross margin flat while letting cash opex rise from 13.0% to 15.0% of revenue, so the deck's price/ARPU swing factor is not carried into the forecast.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified optimism: capex 22% below the guide and 29% below the stated LTM cash capex. Unjustified caution: EBITDA margin fades to 44.5% by FY2030E with no source, and tax is charged on EBIT in loss years. The mirrored scenario shocks themselves are correctly symmetric.

calibration.note: FY2026E EBITDA margin 46.5% vs FY2025A 41.8% in the model is a +4.66pp gap with no qc_justification; it is the reported-to-normalized basis switch, so history and forecast are on different definitions. Section 4 also says the margin rises to the high forties while the model fades it to 44.5%.

signoff.notes: A BUY with +131% on a company that reports a net loss through FY2028E is the one thing to test, and s4 tests it honestly: the loss is the non-cash merger step-up (D&A 44% of revenue falling to 28%), FCFF is positive in FY2027E at Rp6,197bn and the DCF value does not depend on the D&A fade because the add-back and the EBIT charge cancel except through tax. The 84% disagreement between the two methods is disclosed in the leg rather than buried: the EV/EBITDA cross-check strikes 3.77x on the FY2025A reported EBITDA of Rp17,780.9bn which still carries merger and integration cost (company normalised Rp20,100.0bn), the report says plainly that on that base the shares are worth well under half the price and that the same multiple on FY2026E EBITDA roughly reproduces the price, and it weights the DCF 70/30 accordingly. Reverse DCF (FY2027E growth of 3.7% implied against 8.0% forecast) and the sensitivity grid are given; AFFO is computed and the report admits it clears the 7.4% ten-year yield only from FY2028E on a total-capex basis; the IFRS 16 lease double-charge in FCFF plus the net-debt bridge is disclosed as conservative. C1 (capex) was the load-bearing FATAL and it is answered with the Rp20tn guide and Rp10,270bn of 1H2026 capitalised capex, taking FY2026E to 41% of revenue; C2 corrected the peer set, C9 corrected the capex-normalisation language. check PASS. Residual, non-blocking: only two methods carry weight (justified: no dividend today) so the house 'primary plus two cross-checks' line is not met on paper; and Q1 FIX still stands in the text (the 46.5% margin is the FY2026E assumption, the 1H2026 actual prints 46.0%) — rebind it in revision, it does not change the model or the target.

bias.note: Neutral both ways. FY2026E capex of 41% of revenue is the company own raised Rp20tn guide [S8] and the Rp10.27tn capitalised in 1H2026 runs at exactly that rate [S3]; FY2026E revenue growth of 14% and FY2027E of 8% sit below the printed 1H2026 run-rate (+26% yoy; 2 x 24,030 = 48,060 against 48,450) [S19]; the 46.5% margin is a 0.5pp premium to the 1H2026 actual 46.0% [S19] but below the FY2025 normalised 47.3% [S9], derived from cash opex held at 13.0% between the 12.2% FY2025 normalised and 13.5% 1H2026 actual, so it is framed rather than drifted. Scenarios are mirrored (+/-3pp revenue growth, +/-2pp gross margin, -/+3pp capex) at 50/25/25, base at the 40% floor.

Net debt at 30 Jun 2026, IDR bn

findings.finding: Rendered summary (line 44) and section 3 (line 94) state the 1H2026 normalised margin as 46.5% and call it the level the 1H2026 actual prints. F10/F9 give 11,050/24,030 = 45.98% and S19 prints margin 46%; 46.5% is the FY2026E forecast produced by holding cash opex at 13.0%, and the qc_justifications and the opex input both state 46.0% correctly. Both sentences bind fin.FY2026E.ebitda_margin where the half-year actual is meant, so the report overstates the last actual anchor by 0.5pp and the section 3 statement that the compression is a bit over a percentage point is inconsistent with the printed 46.5%.

Section 5 says governance is the reason the valuation carries a discount rather than a full peer multiple, but the engine applies the peer median 3.77x with no discount (multiples.ev_ebitda 3.7699) and sections 4 and 6 correctly say no premium is applied. The reader is told two different things about one multiple.

The engine calibration gate still prints FY2025A 41.8% against FY2026E 46.5%, gap 4.66pp, because history is reported EBITDA (17,780.9) while the forecast is normalised. Section 3 now discloses this properly and gives the like-for-like 47.0% to 46.5%. The mix is defensible because S9 discloses no normalised EBIT or D&A, but the gate will keep firing and must not be read as a margin fade.

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -16.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: opex_pct includes D&A, so the 16pp decline is the D&A ratio easing from 44% to 28% of revenue as the merger fair-value step-ups and the accelerated 900 MHz depreciation roll off [S18]; cash opex (opex_pct less da_pct) is held at 13.0% of revenue for the whole path, between the FY2025 normalized 12.2% and the 1H2026 actual 13.5%, so the EBITDA margin is flat at 46.5% rather than faded [S9][S19].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -13.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: FY2026E 41% of revenue is the company's own raised guide of Rp20tn, and the Rp10.27tn of capitalized capex already spent in 1H2026 runs at exactly that rate [S8][S3]. The 13pp decline to 28% by 2035 is the 101-city 5G build completing, after which capex converges on the model's 28% D&A ratio so the asset base is replaced rather than harvested; it still sits above the 21.4% pre-merger XL standalone ratio because the merged network carries 217 MHz and two brands [S7][S4].

flags.message: a.payout moves +30.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 30% long-run payout is our assumption, not the continuation of the last payment: December 2025 paid Rp2.89tn (Rp159 per share) against Rp3.0tn of normalized profit, a payout of almost the whole normalised year, which is not a policy to extrapolate into a capex-heavy build [S11][S9][S17]. Payout is zero while the FY2025 loss and integration capex absorb cash, then 20% in FY2028E rising to 30% once normalized profit and free cash flow recover; no archived source states a dividend policy, so we label it the house assumption rather than company guidance.

flags.message: expected return +131%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return rests on three sourced inputs, not on a re-rating: (1) capex at the company's own Rp20tn guide for 2026, 41% of revenue, falling to 28% once the 101-city 5G build completes [S8][S3]; (2) the normalized EBITDA margin held flat at 46.5%, the 1H2026 actual (46.0%) and just below the FY2025 normalized level (47.3%), instead of an unsourced fade [S9][S19]; (3) ARPU repair already printed at Rp47.1k vs Rp38.2k a year earlier, carrying 8% FY2027E revenue growth [S19]. What the price implies: the reverse DCF needs only 3.7% FY2027E revenue growth, about half our path [S0]. The multiple does not support the bear reading either way: the stock trades at 4.9x FY2025A reported EBITDA and 4.1x our FY2026E EBITDA against a 3.8x mobile peer median. Applying that median to FY2025A reported EBITDA gives Rp576 per share, 61% BELOW the Rp1,495 price, and applying it to FY2026E normalized EBITDA gives about Rp1,560, roughly the price — so the multiple is sensitive to the EBITDA base and says the market is approximately right on our forward number, not that it is underpricing the D&A step-up [S0][S9]. The DCF premium therefore comes from the capex normalisation and the ARPU repair, which the multiple cannot see.
